mainTopic: Dissolving an oath after eating: רבא's כזית rule, the נזירות challenge, אמימר's view, and a conditional oath on two loaves
overview: This amud continues רבא's ruling that someone who swore off a loaf can have the oath dissolved if he left over a כזית. The גמרא asks why a full כזית is needed, and answers in two ways depending on whether the oath was 'שלא אוכל' or 'שלא אוכלנה'. Next it challenges רבא's assumption that once the whole loaf is eaten, it is too late to dissolve the oath. The challenge comes from a ברייתא about a person with two נזירות vows who dissolved the first one after finishing it. The גמרא first tries to limit that case, and then רב אשי explains that נזירות is different, because dissolving the first lets the kept days count for the second. אמימר disagrees with רבא and holds that one may ask even after eating the whole loaf, since the קרבן or מלקות is still ahead of him. אמימר adds that once a person is tied for lashes it is too late, but the גמרא rejects that limit, since he has not run away. Finally, רבא rules on a conditional oath about two loaves, where liability depends on whether each loaf was eaten by accident or on purpose.

steps.title: Why must a full olive-size piece be left?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא needs a full כזית left over. Even a tiny leftover should be enough to allow dissolving the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if he left any small amount, it should also work!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the detail in רבא's ruling that a כזית must be left over. It argues that any leftover at all should be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the oath has not been fully broken while part of the loaf remains, then even a crumb left over should keep it open to dissolving. So why does רבא say specifically a כזית? The question targets the exact measurement in the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Any amount at all, even a tiny bit
An olive-size amount, the basic measure for 'eating' in halacha

phrases.english: Even any amount, too!
phrases.notes: He means: why did רבא need a full כזית left? Leaving even a crumb should be enough to still dissolve the oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the כזית detail in רבא's ruling, which was stated just before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's requirement that a כזית of the loaf be left over
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If what matters is that the oath is not yet fully broken, any leftover amount should be enough. A full כזית should not be needed.

steps.title: Two possible wordings of the oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets up two ways to explain רבא: either the oath was 'I will not eat' or it was 'I will not eat it'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say the oath was 'I will not eat [this loaf]'; if you want, say the oath was 'I will not eat it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its answer. It gives two possible wordings of the oath and will explain each one in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason a כזית is needed depends on the exact words of the oath. 'שלא אוכל' forbids eating any amount from the loaf. 'שלא אוכלנה' forbids eating the loaf as a whole. Each wording will get its own explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces one of several possible answers
That I will not eat: forbids eating any of it
That I will not eat it: points to the loaf as a whole

phrases.english: If you want, say: 'that I will not eat,'
phrases.notes: Meaning he swore not to eat from this loaf at all.

phrases.english: if you want, say: 'that I will not eat it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge by showing that the answer depends on how the oath was worded
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the case into two possible oath wordings
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any leftover should be enough to allow dissolving the oath
steps.terutzMaskana: The כזית requirement can be explained under either wording, as the next two steps show

steps.title: First wording: the last olive-size piece carries the first
steps.stepSummary: If he swore 'I will not eat,' every כזית is forbidden. Because dissolving still works for the last כזית, it also works for the first one he already ate.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say the oath was 'I will not eat': since asking to dissolve still helps him for the last כזית, it also helps him for the first כזית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first wording. A real כזית must remain so the dissolving has something to take hold of, and then it reaches back to the parts already eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'שלא אוכל,' eating any כזית is a violation, so he already broke the oath with the first כזית. But the last remaining כזית is still a real forbidden 'eating,' so the שאלה is still useful for it. Through מיגו (since it works there), it also works for the earlier pieces. Less than a כזית is not 'eating,' so it could not anchor the שאלה.

keyTerms.meaning: Since: since it works in one case, it works in the other too
Asking a חכם to dissolve an oath or vow

phrases.english: If you want, say: 'that I will not eat':

phrases.aramaic: מִיגּוֹ דְּמַהְנְיָא לֵיהּ שְׁאֵלָה אַכְּזַיִת בָּתְרָא,
phrases.english: since asking for dissolving works for him on the last olive-size piece,

phrases.aramaic: מַהְנְיָא לֵיהּ שְׁאֵלָה נָמֵי אַכְּזַיִת קַמָּא.
phrases.english: asking for dissolving also works for him on the first olive-size piece.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first of the two wordings introduced in step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: מיגו: the dissolving that works for the remaining כזית carries over to the parts already eaten
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any leftover should keep the oath open to dissolving
steps.terutzMaskana: A full כזית is needed because only a real forbidden 'eating' can anchor the שאלה, which then reaches back to what was already eaten

steps.title: Second wording: less than an olive-size is too small to matter
steps.stepSummary: If he swore 'I will not eat it,' a leftover of a כזית is important enough to ask about. A smaller leftover is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say the oath was 'I will not eat it': if he left a כזית, it is important enough to ask a חכם to dissolve the oath for it. If not, it is not important enough to ask about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second wording. Here the only problem with a tiny leftover is that it is too small to be worth a request to dissolve.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'שלא אוכלנה,' the oath is about the whole loaf, so he has not broken it until he finishes. Still, a leftover smaller than a כזית is too unimportant to count, so a שאלה about it means nothing. A כזית is the smallest amount that is חשיב (significant).
steps.whatToRemember: Under either wording of the oath, a full כזית must be left. With 'שלא אוכל,' the last כזית carries the dissolving back to what was already eaten. With 'שלא אוכלנה,' anything less than a כזית is too unimportant to ask about.

phrases.english: And if you want, say: 'that I will not eat it':
if he left over an olive-size piece,
it is significant enough to request dissolving over it;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא, לָא חֲשִׁיב לְאִיתְּשׁוֹלֵי עֲלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and if not, it is not significant enough to request dissolving over it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second explanation, based on the other wording from step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Significance threshold: less than a כזית is not worth a שאלה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the oath is not broken until the loaf is finished, even a crumb should be enough
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a leftover of at least a כזית is important enough to ask about

steps.title: Challenge: a finished נזירות vow can still be dissolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא from a ברייתא. A person with two נזירות vows finished the first one and then had it dissolved, which shows dissolving works even after the vow is completely done.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: One who vowed two terms of נזירות, counted the first term and set aside a קרבן for it, and afterward asked to dissolve the first vow: the second term is counted for him in place of the first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רבא's assumption that once the whole loaf is eaten, the oath can no longer be dissolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the first נזירות was completely finished, even to the point of setting aside its קרבן. Yet the שאלה still worked, and the days he kept now count toward the second vow. So a vow or oath that is fully over can still be dissolved, which seems to go against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow to be a נזיר for a set term
Counted, finished counting the days of the term

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'the second counted in the first' as if he must now keep extra days. It means the days he already kept become the fulfillment of his second vow, so he is not obligated in a further term.

phrases.english: They challenged: one who vowed two terms of naziriteship,
and counted the first and set aside an offering for it,
and afterward asked to dissolve the first:
the second is counted for him in the first!
phrases.notes: The days he already kept now count for the second vow, so he is done.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the כזית question, the גמרא challenges רבא's basic assumption that a fully finished oath cannot be dissolved
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's assumption that once the whole loaf is eaten, the oath can no longer be dissolved
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא shows that a נזירות vow that was fully completed, with its קרבן already set aside, could still be dissolved. So finishing something should not block a שאלה.

steps.title: The נזיר had not yet brought his offerings
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about a נזיר who has not yet brought his end-of-נזירות offerings, so his first נזירות is not truly finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? One where he has not yet brought his atonement offerings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by narrowing the ברייתא. The נזיר had not yet brought his קרבנות, so the first נזירות was not completely over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said you cannot dissolve a vow that is totally done. This answer says the first נזירות was not totally done, because the closing קרבנות were still missing. So the vow was still 'alive' and could be dissolved.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
He atoned, meaning he brought the offerings that end the נזירות
The vow to be a נזיר

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
Where he has not yet atoned.
phrases.notes: 'Atoned' here means bringing the קרבנות a נזיר brings when his term ends.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא in step 5 by limiting its case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that a vow can be dissolved even after it is completely finished.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first נזירות was not fully finished, since its קרבנות had not yet been brought.

steps.title: A teaching says even after offerings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: a ברייתא explicitly says this works even after he brought the offerings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the previous answer. A ברייתא says the dissolving works even after he already brought his קרבנות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא includes a case where the offerings were already brought, then the answer of step 6 does not fit. We are back to a vow that seems fully finished and yet still gets dissolved.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: he atoned!
phrases.notes: He means a ברייתא that says the dissolving works even after he brought the קרבנות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the limitation offered in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא is about one who had not yet brought his offerings.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly includes the case after the offerings, so the limitation fails.

steps.title: He had not yet shaved, following רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The case is where he brought the offerings but did not yet shave. According to רבי אליעזר, shaving is required to finish the נזירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where he had not shaved, and it follows רבי אליעזר, who says shaving is indispensable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new narrower case. He brought the offerings but had not yet shaved his hair. This follows רבי אליעזר, who holds the נזירות is not complete without shaving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is the same as before: the first נזירות was still not completely over. This time the missing piece is the shaving instead of the offerings. That only works according to רבי אליעזר, who says the shaving holds back the completion.

keyTerms.meaning: He shaved (the נזיר's hair at the end of his term)
Holds back, is indispensable for completion

phrases.english: Where he has not shaved,
and it is the view of Rabbi Eliezer,
who says shaving is indispensable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 with a later stage that is still incomplete.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new limitation of the case, tied to one opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once the offerings were brought, the נזירות is fully over.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי אליעזר, the נזירות is not over until he shaves, so it can still be dissolved.

steps.title: A teaching says even after shaving
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects again: a ברייתא says it works even after he shaved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. A ברייתא says the dissolving works even after he already shaved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now no step of the נזירות is left to finish. It looks like the vow really was totally complete and was still dissolved, which goes against רבא.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: he shaved!

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that he had not yet shaved.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא includes even the case after shaving, so nothing of the נזירות remains incomplete.

steps.title: נזירות is different from oaths
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that two נזירות are a special case. The first one is what held back the second, so dissolving the first just lets the second take its place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Are you comparing נזירות to oaths? What kept the second from taking effect? The first. And now it is gone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי stops trying to limit the ברייתא. He says you cannot compare נזירות to an oath at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only thing delaying the second נזירות was the first one. Once the first is dissolved, the days he kept count toward the second, so the vow still has a real effect. With the oath, once the loaf is eaten nothing is left for the vow to affect.

keyTerms.meaning: You are comparing / setting one against the other

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying an offering or the shaving was still missing. His point is that the days he kept can count just as well for the second נזירות, so once the first is dissolved it can be treated as if it never started. An eaten loaf has nothing like that to fall back on.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves רבא's rule. A finished vow cannot be dissolved unless dissolving it still has some real effect.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Are you comparing nazirite vows?
What caused the second not to take effect?
The first; and it is no longer there.
phrases.notes: Once the first is dissolved, it's as if it never was, so his days count for the second.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: נְזִירוֹת קָא רָמֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives up on limiting the case and instead shows the ברייתא cannot be compared to oaths.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא proves that even a fully finished vow can be dissolved, against רבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: With two נזירות, dissolving the first still matters because it frees the second to take effect. An eaten loaf leaves nothing for the oath to affect.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא survives: a fully finished oath cannot be dissolved. The two-נזירות case works only because dissolving the first still has an effect on the second.

steps.title: אמימר: even after eating it all
steps.stepSummary: אמימר disagrees with רבא. Even if he ate the whole loaf, he can ask for התרה, because the קרבן or the lashes are still ahead of him.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: Even if he ate all of it, he may ask for התרה. If by mistake, he still owes a קרבן. If on purpose, he still owes lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא, אמימר, gives a different view from רבא. One can ask to dissolve the oath even after eating the entire loaf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אמימר, the oath is not 'dead' as long as a result of breaking it is still pending. If he ate by mistake, he still has to bring a קרבן. If he ate on purpose, he still has to get מלקות. Dissolving the oath would cancel those.

keyTerms.meaning: He may ask (a חכם) to dissolve it
Still lacking, has not yet received

phrases.english: Ameimar said:
Even if he ate all of it, he may ask about it;
phrases.notes: 'It' is the loaf from רבא's oath case.

phrases.english: if unwittingly, he still lacks the offering,
if intentionally, he still lacks lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opinion that argues with רבא's whole position.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath can be dissolved even after it was completely broken, as long as the קרבן or מלקות has not yet happened.

steps.title: Too late once tied for lashes, like שמואל
steps.stepSummary: אמימר limits his rule. Once he is tied to the post for lashes, he can no longer ask, because שמואל holds that being tied counts as the punishment starting.
steps.simpleTranslation: But once they tied him to the post, no. This follows שמואל, who said: if they tied him to the post and he ran away from בית דין, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר sets a limit on his rule and supports it with שמואל. Once he has been tied to the post for lashes, it is too late to ask.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל says a person tied to the post who escapes is exempt, so being tied already counts like receiving the lashes. That means nothing is pending anymore. With nothing left for the oath to affect, it can no longer be dissolved.

keyTerms.meaning: The post a person is tied to for lashes

steps.whatToRemember: רבא: once the whole loaf is eaten, the oath can no longer be dissolved, so a כזית must be left. אמימר: it can be dissolved even after he ate it all, because the קרבן or lashes are still ahead of him.

phrases.english: But if they tied him to the post, no;
like Shmuel, as Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּפָתוּהוּ עַל הָעַמּוּד וְרָץ מִבֵּית דִּין –
phrases.english: If they tied him to the post and he ran from the court,
he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Being tied already counts as the lashes starting, so he isn't brought back for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts a limit on אמימר's rule from step 11 and backs it with שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once he is tied to the post for lashes, the oath can no longer be dissolved, since the punishment counts as already begun.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל: one tied to the post who ran from בית דין is exempt.

steps.title: Being tied does not stop him from asking, because he did not run away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects אמימר's limitation. שמואל's case was about someone who ran away after being tied, but here the person has not run away.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not correct. There, he ran away. Here, he did not run away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 12. It says that even someone already tied for lashes can still ask a חכם to dissolve his oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said being tied counts as the punishment starting only for someone who ran away. Since the beating had begun, he does not need a new one. Our person is still standing there facing the lashes, so the punishment is still ahead of him, and he can still ask for התרה.

keyTerms.meaning: And that is not so: a phrase the גמרא uses to reject an idea it just said
There, meaning in the other case

steps.whatToRemember: Within אמימר's approach, the conclusion is that a person can ask for התרה even while tied for lashes, as long as he has not run away.

phrases.english: And that is not so;
phrases.notes: This rejects אמימר's limit from the step before, that being tied stops him from asking.

phrases.english: there, he ran away,
phrases.notes: "There" is שמואל's case: he was tied, then escaped, so he is not tied again.

phrases.english: here, he did not run away.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא הִיא; הָתָם רָץ, הָכָא לָא רָץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the limitation added in step 12 by showing that שמואל's rule applies to a different case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects אמימר's claim that being tied to the post ends the chance to ask for התרה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שמואל's rule was about someone who ran away after being tied. A person who did not run away is still facing the punishment.

steps.title: A conditional oath about two loaves: accident versus on purpose
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules on the oath 'I will not eat this loaf if I eat that one.' Of the cases he lists, he is liable only when he ate the condition loaf on purpose and the forbidden loaf by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone said, 'I swear I will not eat this loaf if I eat that one,' and he ate the first loaf by accident and the second on purpose, he is exempt. If he ate the first on purpose and the second by accident, he is liable. If he ate both by accident, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: a שבועה that only takes effect if a condition is met. רבא goes through the different combinations of eating by accident and on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key is the first loaf eaten, the condition loaf. If he ate it by accident, the condition was not met with full intent, so the oath never takes effect and he is exempt. If he ate it on purpose, the oath takes effect, and then eating the second loaf by accident makes him liable to bring a קרבן for breaking an oath by accident.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable, responsible to bring a קרבן

steps.confusionAlert: "The first" loaf means the loaf he ate first, which is the condition loaf. In the wording of the oath it is mentioned second ('if I eat this one').
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a conditional שבועה only takes effect when the condition is fulfilled knowingly. Eating the condition loaf by accident does not turn the oath on.

phrases.english: Rava says:
"On my oath I will not eat this loaf
if I eat this one,"
and he ate the first one by accident
phrases.notes: "The first" means the condition loaf, since that is the one he eats first.

phrases.english: and the second on purpose, he is exempt.
The first on purpose
and the second by accident, he is liable.
Both by accident, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל כִּכָּר זוֹ אִם אוֹכַל זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of התרה and lashes ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A conditional oath takes effect only if the condition loaf was eaten on purpose. He is liable only when the condition loaf was eaten on purpose and the forbidden loaf was eaten by accident. In every other combination listed, he is exempt.
